question.:question/problem:
The vectors $a_{1},a_{2}$ and $b$ are given below. Determine whether $b\in \operatorname{Span}\{a_{1},a_{2}\}$. In the affirmative case, find $x_{1}\cdot x_{2}$ from the decomposition $b=x_{1}a_{1}+x_{2}a_{2}$.
$a_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
$a_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
$b=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
By the definition of span, $b\in \operatorname{Span}\{a_{1},a_{2}\}$ exactly when coefficients exist such that

$$
x_{1}a_{1}+x_{2}a_{2}=b.
$$

Equating components gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x_{2} &= 8 \\ x_{1}+x_{2} &= -4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix and use elementary row operations:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}0 & -2 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & -4\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{1}\leftrightarrow R_{2}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{array}\right]
$$

Back-substitution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x_{2} &= \frac{8}{-2} = -4 \\ x_{1} &= \frac{-4-\left(1\right)\left(-4\right)}{1} = 0\end{aligned}
$$

All component equations hold. Thus $b\in \operatorname{Span}\{a_{1},a_{2}\}$ and the coefficients are unique. Finally,

$$
x_{1}\cdot x_{2}=\left(0\right)\cdot \left(-4\right)=0.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Determine whether $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, where $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}&=\langle 0, 3, 1\rangle \\ \mathbf{c}&=\langle 1, -3, 0\rangle \\ \mathbf{u}&=\langle 2, -15, -3\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

If it does, select the value of $s\cdot t$ in $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$. Otherwise, select the statement that $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$.

Use the component equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}t &=2 \\ 3s-3t &=-15 \\ s &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

**Check all three coordinates.** Use the equations that isolate the coefficients, then verify the remaining equation.
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in\Pi$ exactly when the same values of $s$ and $t$ satisfy all three coordinate equations. Expanding the vector equation gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}t &=2 \\ 3s-3t &=-15 \\ s &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -3 & -15 \\ 1 & 0 & -3\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)R_1$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-(1)R_2$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}3 & -3 & -15 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row is $0=0$, so it adds no restriction. Back substitute in the two nonzero rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{2}{1}=2 \\ s&=\frac{-15-(-3)(2)}{3}=-3\end{aligned}
$$

- $(C+A)B=BC+AB$ is **not always true**. Distribute with the outside factor on the same side in each product.

$$
\begin{aligned}(C+A)B &=CB+AB\end{aligned}
$$

The proposed right side is not guaranteed to equal this result. For example, take

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\quad B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\quad C=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then the left side is $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ and the proposed right side is $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, so this is a counterexample.

- $C(BA)=(CB)A$ is **always true**. Associativity moves parentheses while retaining the order of every factor.

$$
\begin{aligned}C(BA) &=(CB)A\end{aligned}
$$

- $I_2C=I_2$ is **not always true**. The identity factor disappears; the arbitrary matrix remains.

$$
\begin{aligned}I_2C &=C\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Then the left side is $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ and the proposed right side is $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, so this is a counterexample.

Select $C(BA)=(CB)A$.
